Neonatal Great spotted cuckoos emerge from the egg at a modest size, with newly hatched chicks weighing approximately 7 grams [Wwb = approximately 7 grams]. This initial mass, typical of many obligate brood parasites, belies the rapid growth trajectory the nestling must sustain to compete with host siblings. The incubation period, derived from comparative data on the common cuckoo Cuculus canoris, proceeds at an internal egg temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], yielding an age at hatching of about 13.5 days [ab = about 13.5 days]. This relatively short incubation is consistent with the altricial mode of development found across many cuckoo species. Field observations indicate that the nestling phase culminates in fledging, which under the elevated body temperatures typical of active metabolic periods in this species, measured at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], occurs a mere 20.3 days after hatching [tx = 20.3 days after hatching]. This rapid fledging interval is an adaptation to minimize the duration of exposure to host aggression and predation risk within the nest.

As the juvenile cuckoo transitions toward independence, somatic growth continues until the adult body form is fully realized. The ultimate wet weight, representing the asymptotic mass of a fully grown adult, reaches approximately 133 grams [Wwi = approximately 133 grams]. This body size places the Great spotted cuckoo at an intermediate position among the Cuculinae, heavier than the diminutive Dideric cuckoo but substantially lighter than the larger channel-billed cuckoo. Attainment of this adult mass is a prerequisite for the onset of reproductive competence. At the same maintained body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], which reflects the standard thermal regime of an actively foraging adult bird, puberty is achieved at 60.9 days since birth [tp = 60.9 days since birth]. This relatively brief pre-reproductive period is notable for a brood parasite, as early sexual maturation facilitates rapid population turnover and the exploitation of ephemeral host breeding opportunities.

The timing of first breeding represents a critical life-history milestone for the Great spotted cuckoo, as it directly influences generation time and population growth potential. Under the consistent thermal conditions of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], which typify the core body temperature of an active adult passerine, the first successful brood is initiated at 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth]. This precise annual cycle aligns the onset of reproduction with the peak breeding season of its primary hosts, magpies of the genus Pica, ensuring a ready supply of suitable nests for parasitism. The interval between sexual maturity at 60.9 days and first reproduction at one year is devoted to territory establishment, host searching, and the development of the precise egg-laying coordination required for successful parasitism. This delay is not uncommon among cuckoos, which often require an extended period to learn the spatial distribution of host territories.

Reproductive output in the Great spotted cuckoo is constrained by both clutch size and the frequency of nesting attempts within a season. Females typically produce 1 to 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 2 eggs per clutch], a modest fecundity that reflects the high energy cost of producing mimetic eggs that evade host detection. Field studies conducted in Mediterranean populations indicate that individual females manage approximately 1.5 clutches annually [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 clutches annually], spread across the extended breeding season of their corvid hosts. This relatively low annual reproductive effort is compensated by a high rate of chick survival, as the cuckoo nestling typically outcompetes or evicts host young. This corresponds to a daily reproduction rate of approximately 0.055 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 0.055 eggs per day] based on the product of clutch size and frequency divided by 365. The long-term consequences of this reproductive strategy are reflected in the maximum lifespan, which at a standard body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], is estimated at 4709 days [am = 4709 days]. This longevity, exceeding twelve years, is substantial for a bird of this body mass and suggests a slow pace of life relative to many other passeriforms.

Comparative analyses of the Great spotted cuckoo's life history reveal several intriguing contrasts with related brood parasites. Its maximum recorded longevity, inferred from field studies of the common cuckoo and estimated at 4709 days [am = 4709 days] at the typical avian body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], exceeds that predicted by allometric scaling relationships for a bird with an ultimate adult mass of 133 grams [Wwi = 133 grams]. This extended survival may be linked to a relatively low annual reproductive rate, as the trade-off between current reproduction and future survival is well documented in long-lived birds. The species also exhibits notable behavioral plasticity; individual females have been observed to parasitize multiple host species within a single season, adjusting egg phenotype accordingly. Such flexibility likely buffers the population against fluctuations in the abundance of any single host, contributing to the remarkable persistence of Clamator glandarius across its wide Palaearctic and Afrotropical range. These ecological considerations underscore the intricate interplay between physiology, behavior, and demography that characterizes this specialized brood parasite.
